children: Wall Street investors expecting a rally after the November midterm elections may be disappointed, according to BTIG strategist Jonathan Krinsky, who sees growing risks of a stock-market decline as credit conditions deteriorate and several sectors show signs of weakness.
The S&P 500 (

) could retreat toward 7,300, near its 200-day moving average and summer lows, Krinsky said Sunday in a research report. That would represent a decline of about 4.3% from the index's recent level of 7,631. The benchmark could fall further if it breaks below that technical support level.

The warning challenges the widely held expectation that stocks will rally once uncertainty surrounding the November 3 elections has passed. Historically, midterm elections have often marked a turning point for equities, but Krinsky argues that the market's unusually strong performance this year makes a repeat less likely.
Since 1962, the S&P 500 (

) has experienced an average maximum drawdown of 13.76% during the June-to-December period of midterm election years, according to BTIG. This year, the largest decline since June 1 has been just 4.5%, the second-smallest over that period.
"The reason stocks often perform well in November during midterms is because SPX typically is weak INTO the elections," Krinsky wrote. "We have the opposite setup this year."
The strategist said the S&P 500 (
) has also moved against its historical seasonal pattern at other points this year, suggesting investors shouldn't assume the election will provide a catalyst for further gains.
"While consensus is that we see a post midterm rally, we think the opposite is actually more likely," he wrote.
Credit markets flash warning signs
One of Krinsky's biggest concerns is the widening gap between yields on lower-rated corporate debt, a development that can signal growing financial stress before it becomes apparent in stock prices.
The spread between bonds rated B and CCC has reached approximately 7.8 percentage points, a level seen only four other times since 1996, according to BTIG.

image.alt: Junk spreads continue to blow out.

children: In each previous instance, the S&P 500 (SP500) was already at least 11.8% below its 52-week high. In two cases, the benchmark had fallen about 30% by the time credit spreads reached comparable levels.
The current divergence is striking because the S&P 500 (SP500) remains only about 2% below its recent high.
"So, either 'it's different this time', or SPX is likely in for some rough sledding," Krinsky wrote.

For investors, the disconnect raises questions about whether equity valuations adequately reflect deteriorating credit conditions. Wider spreads can indicate growing concern about corporate borrowers' ability to repay debt, potentially foreshadowing tighter financing conditions and weaker economic activity.

Krinsky also identified growing stress in technology credit markets. Credit-default swap spreads for major hyperscale computing companies continue to widen, while investment-grade technology credit spreads have reached their highest levels since 2022.
That deterioration comes even as the S&P 500 technology sector
trades only a few percentage points below record highs.

Private-credit markets are showing similar weakness. Business development companies, which provide financing to businesses outside traditional bank lending channels, have fallen to multiyear lows and have struggled to sustain rallies.
Semiconductor weakness contrasts with software strength
Krinsky remains bearish on semiconductor stocks after a recent attempt to rebound from technical support failed.
Although the iShares Semiconductor ETF
and VanEck Semiconductor ETF
remain above their 200-day moving averages, the SPDR S&P Semiconductor ETF
, which uses an equal-weight methodology, has already broken below that level.
"We continue to think semis work lower over the coming weeks and months," Krinsky wrote.

Software stocks, however, represent a potential bright spot. An equal-weight software index has broken out of a two-year trading range, with relative strength against the broader market reaching its highest level this year.
The ratio of equal-weight software stocks to equal-weight semiconductor stocks has also broken above a yearlong trading base, suggesting a possible shift in leadership within technology.
"If looking for momentum, this is the spot," Krinsky wrote of software.
The divergence suggests investors may need to become more selective within technology rather than treating the sector as a single trade.
Lack of investor fear adds to concerns
Krinsky also questioned whether the market has experienced enough selling pressure to establish a durable bottom.

Options-market put/call ratios remain substantially below the levels reached during periods of market stress in March and July, suggesting investors haven't aggressively purchased protection against further declines.
"Hard to think we have seen a meaningful low when there is a lack of hedging," he wrote.

Market breadth provides another warning. On approximately 33% of trading days this year, the S&P 500's direction has differed from the direction of market breadth, meaning the index has risen while more stocks declined or vice versa.
BTIG's historical analysis suggests such a persistent divergence is unlikely to continue indefinitely.
Several economically sensitive industries also appear vulnerable. Krinsky identified industrials
, healthcare
, restaurants, airlines
and casinos
as groups showing technical weakness.
The report highlighted Chipotle Mexican Grill
, whose shares have retreated to levels last seen in 2022. BTIG separately maintains a Buy rating and $45 price target on the restaurant chain.

Taken together, the weakening credit indicators, deteriorating market breadth and technical breakdowns across multiple sectors suggest that investors may be underestimating the risk of a broader correction.

Rather than marking the end of market uncertainty, the midterm elections could coincide with renewed selling pressure, particularly if the S&P 500 (SP500) follows other major market segments in testing its 200-day moving average.

title: BTIG warns stocks may fall after midterms as credit risks mount
